bibl.title: Microbiome definition re-visited: old concepts and new challenges

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: ONE WORD, AND THE TWELVE PUBLISHED DEFINITIONS OF IT - `microbiome`, catalogued into ecological, host-dependent, genomic/method-driven and combined families, each family's characteristic failure named
span.quote: As a result of this rapid growth in interest covering different fields, we are lacking a clear commonly agreed definition of the term “microbiome.” Moreover, a consensus on best practices in microbiome research is missing.

span.label: what `microbiome` should mean, when a field spanning agriculture, medicine, ecology and biotechnology has no agreed definition and its experts cannot agree who the members are
span.quote: The lack of data standardization as a matter of continuous development of new techniques and equipment, as well as the urgent need for better coordination and collaboration across the field of microbiome research, was recently listed as the most important challenges facing microbiome researchers [ 2 ]. Furthermore, a consistent criticism has been that microbiome research is more driven by methods than by hypotheses or concepts [ 24 ]. To provide mechanistic insights in microbiota functioning is not only important for the human microbiome, it affects all areas in this research field. However, a clear or consensus definition of “microbiome” among researchers from diverse fields remains debatable

span.label: the REVIVAL of Whipps et al.'s 1988 definition, extended by two sentences that separate `microbiome` from `microbiota` and assert its dynamic character, plus six amendments agreed by about 40 workshop participants and over a hundred survey respondents
span.quote: Based on the recent advances in the area, we suggest the revival of the original definition of the microbiome term suggested by Whipps et al. [ 40 ]. The definition, which contains all important points that are valid even 30 years after its publication in 1988, was extended by two explanatory sentences differentiating the terms microbiome and microbiota and pronouncing its dynamic character.

span.label: method
span.quote: The microbiome is defined as a characteristic microbial community occupying a reasonable well-defined habitat which has distinct physio-chemical properties. The microbiome not only refers to the microorganisms involved but also encompass their theatre of activity, which results in the formation of specific ecological niches. The microbiome, which forms a dynamic and interactive micro-ecosystem prone to change in time and scale, is integrated in macro-ecosystems including eukaryotic hosts, and here crucial for their functioning and health. The microbiota consists of the assembly of microorganisms belonging to different kingdoms (Prokaryotes [Bacteria, Archaea], Eukaryotes [e.g., Protozoa, Fungi, and Algae]), while “their theatre of activity” includes microbial structures, metabolites, mobile genetic elements (e.g., transposons, phages, and viruses), and relic DNA embedded in the environmental conditions of the habitat.

span.label: a term whose definition families each fail differently, and one of which must fail again with every new instrument
span.quote: Genomic/ method-driven definitions There is a variety of microbiome definitions available that are driven by the methods applied. Mostly, these definitions rely on DNA sequence-based analysis and describe microbiome as a collective genome of microorganisms in a specific environment. The main bottleneck here is that every new available technology will result in a need for a new definition.

span.label: an expert workshop (about 40 leaders, Tulln, 6 March 2019, MicrobiomeSupport) plus an online survey answered by more than a hundred experts worldwide, against a catalogue of the published definitions and a historical review
span.term: an expert workshop (about 40 leaders, Tulln, 6 March 2019, MicrobiomeSupport) plus an online survey answered by more than a hundred experts worldwide, against a catalogue of the published definitions and a historical review
span.quote: As a result of this rapid growth in interest covering different fields, we are lacking a clear commonly agreed definition of the term “microbiome.” Moreover, a consensus on best practices in microbiome research is missing.

span.label: **A DEFINITION FAMILY WHOSE INSTABILITY IS STRUCTURAL**: `There is a variety of microbiome definitions available THAT ARE DRIVEN BY THE METHODS APPLIED. Mostly, these definitions rely on DNA sequence-based analysis and describe microbiome as a collective genome of microorganisms in a specific environment. THE MAIN BOTTLENECK HERE IS THAT EVERY NEW AVAILABLE TECHNOLOGY WILL RESULT IN A NEED FOR A NEW DEFINITION.` The sharpest sentence about definitions in this corpus: a family of definitions keyed to the instrument, and therefore guaranteed to be obsoleted by the next one
span.quote: Genomic/ method-driven definitions There is a variety of microbiome definitions available that are driven by the methods applied. Mostly, these definitions rely on DNA sequence-based analysis and describe microbiome as a collective genome of microorganisms in a specific environment. The main bottleneck here is that every new available technology will result in a need for a new definition.

span.label: AND THE OTHER FAMILIES FAIL DIFFERENTLY, EACH WITH ITS GAP NAMED: ECOLOGICAL - `the theories from the macro-ecology DO NOT ALWAYS FIT THE RULES IN THE MICROBIAL WORLD`; HOST-DEPENDENT - `whether the microbial-host interaction data gained from ONE HOST CAN BE TRANSFERRED TO ANOTHER ... The understanding of coevolution and selection in the host-dependent definitions is also UNDERREPRESENTED`. A catalogue of definitions sorted by HOW EACH ONE BREAKS, which is a thing no other record here does
span.quote: Ecological definitions Definitions based on ecology describe the microbiome following the concepts derived from the ecology of multicellular organisms. The main issue here is that the theories from the macro-ecology do not always fit the rules in the microbial world.

span.label: AND THE MOST-CITED DEFINITION IS NOT THE ORIGINAL: the 1988 coinage by Whipps et al. described `the `MICROBIOME` AS A COMBINATION OF THE WORDS `MICRO` AND `BIOME`, naming a `CHARACTERISTIC MICROBIAL COMMUNITY` in a `REASONABLY WELL-DEFINED HABITAT WHICH HAS DISTINCT PHYSIO-CHEMICAL PROPERTIES` as their `THEATRE OF ACTIVITY``, while `THE CURRENTLY MOST CITED DEFINITION BY LEDERBERG describes microbiomes within an ecological context`. The word that won is not the definition that was first
span.quote: In 1988, Whipps and colleagues working on the ecology of rhizosphere microorganisms provided the first definition of the term microbiome [ 40 ]. They described the “microbiome” as a combination of the words “micro” and “biome”, naming a “characteristic microbial community” in a “reasonably well-defined habitat which has distinct physio-chemical properties” as their “theatre of activity” (Table 1 ). This definition represents a substantial advancement of the definition of a microbial community, as it defines a microbial community with distinct properties and functions and its interactions with its environment, resulting in the formation of specific ecological niches.

span.label: **AND A 2020 CONSENSUS THAT REVERTS TO A 1988 DEFINITION**: `we suggest THE REVIVAL OF THE ORIGINAL DEFINITION of the microbiome term suggested by Whipps et al. The definition, which contains all important points that are VALID EVEN 30 YEARS AFTER ITS PUBLICATION IN 1988, WAS EXTENDED BY TWO EXPLANATORY SENTENCES differentiating the terms microbiome and microbiota and pronouncing its dynamic character.` Banff revised forward, GLIS voted a new one, ACR/EULAR replaced five. This body went BACK
span.quote: Based on the recent advances in the area, we suggest the revival of the original definition of the microbiome term suggested by Whipps et al. [ 40 ]. The definition, which contains all important points that are valid even 30 years after its publication in 1988, was extended by two explanatory sentences differentiating the terms microbiome and microbiota and pronouncing its dynamic character.

span.label: **AND THE MEMBERSHIP DISPUTE HAS NO CENTRE**: `The integration of phages, viruses, plasmids, and mobile genetic elements is ONE OF THE MOST CONTROVERSIAL POINTS in the definition of the microbiome ... THE ANSWERS OF THE SURVEY PARTICIPANTS to the question whether viruses and phages should be a part of the microbiome PROVIDED NO CLEAR ANSWER AND STRETCHED FROM `IN ANY CASE` TO `DEFINITELY NO.`` A survey of over a hundred experts returning the full width of the scale
span.quote: The integration of phages, viruses, plasmids, and mobile genetic elements is one of the most controversial points in the definition of the microbiome. This was also confirmed by the participants’ comments in the “microbiome definition” online survey. The answers of the survey participants to the question whether viruses and phages should be a part of the microbiome provided no clear answer and stretched from “in any case” to “definitely no.”

span.label: AND THE DISPUTED MATERIAL IS UP TO 80% OF THE SAMPLE AND CHANGES NOTHING: `RELIC DNA CAN COMPRISE UP TO 40% OF THE SEQUENCED DNA IN SOIL and was UP TO 33% OF THE TOTAL BACTERIAL DNA ON AVERAGE in a broader analysis of habitats WITH THE HIGHEST PROPORTION OF 80% IN SOME SAMPLES. Interestingly, DESPITE ITS OMNIPRESENCE AND ABUNDANCE, RELIC DNA HAD A MINIMAL EFFECT ON ESTIMATES of taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity.` The argument about whether it belongs is not an argument about the numbers
span.quote: There is also no clear consensus as to whether extracellular DNA derived from dead cells (so-called “relic DNA”) belongs to the microbiome. Relic DNA can comprise up to 40% of the sequenced DNA in soil [ 53 ] and was up to 33% of the total bacterial DNA on average in a broader analysis of habitats with the highest proportion of 80% in some samples [ 54 ]. Interestingly, despite its omnipresence and abundance, relic DNA had a minimal effect on estimates of taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity

span.label: **AND THE DISPUTE IS DISSOLVED BY SPLITTING THE TERM**: `a CLEAR DIFFERENTIATION BETWEEN MICROBIOME AND MICROBIOTA HELPS TO AVOID THE CONTROVERSY concerning the members of a microbiome. Microbiota is usually defined as THE ASSEMBLAGE OF LIVING MICROORGANISMS present in a defined environment. As phages, viruses, plasmids, prions, viroids, and free DNA are USUALLY NOT CONSIDERED AS LIVING MICROORGANISMS, THEY DO NOT BELONG TO THE MICROBIOTA.` A terminological split used to settle a substantive disagreement - both sides keep their answer, in different words
span.quote: When it comes to the use of specific terms, a clear differentiation between microbiome and microbiota helps to avoid the controversy concerning the members of a microbiome (Fig. 2 ). Microbiota is usually defined as the assemblage of living microorganisms present in a defined environment [ 25 ]. As phages, viruses, plasmids, prions, viroids, and free DNA are usually not considered as living microorganisms [ 55 ], they do not belong to the microbiota.

span.label: AND A DICTIONARY CARRIES TWO OF THE DEFINITIONS AND NEITHER WORKS: `MERRIAM WEBSTER publishing platform, for example, SUGGESTS TWO MICROBIOME DEFINITIONS: one describing the metagenome and the other is the community of microorganisms, YET STILL FAILS TO CAPTURE THE HOST AND THE ENVIRONMENT as an integral ecological component of the microbiome, rather than an independent entity.` The reference work the public reads holds two senses of the word and the paper rejects both
span.quote: Merriam Webster publishing platform, for example, suggests two microbiome definitions: one describing the metagenome and the other is the community of microorganisms, yet still fails to capture the host and the environment as an integral ecological component of the microbiome, rather than an independent entity.

span.label: AND THE FIELD IS TOLD TO STOP COINING -OME WORDS: `Despite more and more terms like `BACTERIOME,` `ARCHAEOME,` `MYCOBIOME,` OR `VIROME` have started to appear in the scientific literature, THESE TERMS DO NOT REFER TO BIOMES ... Consequently, IT WOULD BE BETTER TO USE THE ORIGINAL TERMS (bacterial, archaeal, or fungal community).` A paper legislating against a productive morphological pattern in its own field - and the reason is that the suffix has stopped meaning what it means
span.quote: Despite more and more terms like “bacteriome,” “archaeome,” “mycobiome,” or “virome” have started to appear in the scientific literature, and these terms do not refer to biomes (a regional ecosystem with a distinct assemblage of (micro) organisms, and physical environment often reflecting a certain climate and soil) as the microbiome itself. Consequently, it would be better to use the original terms (bacterial, archaeal, or fungal community).

span.label: AND A THIRD TERM IS ROUTINELY CONFUSED WITH IT: `The term microbiome is also sometimes CONFUSED WITH THE METAGENOME. Metagenome is, however, CLEARLY DEFINED AS A COLLECTION OF GENOMES AND GENES FROM THE MEMBERS OF A MICROBIOTA.` Three terms - microbiome, microbiota, metagenome - whose separation is the paper's main housekeeping act
span.quote: The term microbiome is also sometimes confused with the metagenome. Metagenome is, however, clearly defined as a collection of genomes and genes from the members of a microbiota

span.label: THE FIELD IS DRIVEN BY METHODS RATHER THAN CONCEPTS, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO ABOUT ITSELF: `THE LACK OF DATA STANDARDIZATION as a matter of continuous development of new techniques and equipment ... was recently listed as THE MOST IMPORTANT CHALLENGES facing microbiome researchers. Furthermore, A CONSISTENT CRITICISM HAS BEEN THAT MICROBIOME RESEARCH IS MORE DRIVEN BY METHODS THAN BY HYPOTHESES OR CONCEPTS ... However, A CLEAR OR CONSENSUS DEFINITION OF `MICROBIOME` AMONG RESEARCHERS FROM DIVERSE FIELDS REMAINS DEBATABLE`
span.quote: The lack of data standardization as a matter of continuous development of new techniques and equipment, as well as the urgent need for better coordination and collaboration across the field of microbiome research, was recently listed as the most important challenges facing microbiome researchers [ 2 ]. Furthermore, a consistent criticism has been that microbiome research is more driven by methods than by hypotheses or concepts [ 24 ]. To provide mechanistic insights in microbiota functioning is not only important for the human microbiome, it affects all areas in this research field. However, a clear or consensus definition of “microbiome” among researchers from diverse fields remains debatable

span.label: AND THERE IS NO INSTRUMENT TO SETTLE IT WITH: `Microbiome research is STRONGLY DRIVEN BY METHODOLOGICAL ADVANCES. Despite all progress in this area, THERE IS NO PERFECT AND UNIVERSAL METHOD. A TOOLBOX OF TECHNOLOGIES WILL REDUCE BIAS RESULTING FROM EACH INDIVIDUAL TECHNOLOGY and result in a more complete view on the biological system as a whole.` The remedy for a method-shaped definition is more methods, not a better one
span.quote: Microbiome research is strongly driven by methodological advances. Despite all progress in this area, there is no perfect and universal method. A toolbox of technologies will reduce bias resulting from each individual technology and result in a more complete view on the biological system as a whole.

span.label: AND THE FIELD'S OWN CLASSIFICATION OF ITS OBJECTS IS CALLED ANTHROPOCENTRIC: `The division of microorganisms into BENEFICIAL, PATHOGENIC, AND NEUTRAL according to microbial interactions with their hosts IS BASED ON AN ANTHROPOCENTRIC VIEW. Indeed, the physiology of the host and the whole microbiome substantially influence the outcome of the interaction.` The same move as piggott2015's `what is stressful to one species is likely to be beneficial to another` - a classification whose categories are a point of view
span.quote: Disease state of the holobiont is characterized by dysbiosis (pathobiome), while eubiosis refers to a balanced host-microbe interaction (“healthy” microbiome). The division of microorganisms into beneficial, pathogenic, and neutral according to microbial interactions with their hosts is based on an anthropocentric view [ 210 ]. Indeed, the physiology of the host and the whole microbiome substantially influence the outcome of the interaction.

span.label: the keystone-species concept is carried from macro-ecology into microbiome research, where hub species in a network are hypothesised to play the same role
span.quote: Hub species in networks are often hypothesized to serve as keystone species, a concept which has been transferred from macro-ecology into microbiome research [ 82 ].

span.label: one whole family of microbiome definitions is built on concepts taken from the ecology of multicellular organisms rather than from microbiology
span.quote: Definitions based on ecology describe the microbiome following the concepts derived from the ecology of multicellular organisms.

span.label: an online survey of more than a hundred experts worldwide, run BEFORE the workshop that agreed the definition
span.note: eliminates: a definition agreed by the forty people who happened to be in the room · outcome: partial
span.quote: As a result of this rapid growth in interest covering different fields, we are lacking a clear commonly agreed definition of the term “microbiome.” Moreover, a consensus on best practices in microbiome research is missing.

span.label: cataloguing the existing published definitions into four families and naming each family's characteristic failure before proposing anything
span.note: eliminates: a new definition offered without an account of why the existing ones did not hold · outcome: held
span.quote: Genomic/ method-driven definitions There is a variety of microbiome definitions available that are driven by the methods applied. Mostly, these definitions rely on DNA sequence-based analysis and describe microbiome as a collective genome of microorganisms in a specific environment. The main bottleneck here is that every new available technology will result in a need for a new definition.

span.label: separating `microbiome` from `microbiota` so that the disputed members sit on a named side
span.note: eliminates: the unresolvable argument about whether viruses, phages and relic DNA are members · outcome: held
span.quote: When it comes to the use of specific terms, a clear differentiation between microbiome and microbiota helps to avoid the controversy concerning the members of a microbiome (Fig. 2 ). Microbiota is usually defined as the assemblage of living microorganisms present in a defined environment [ 25 ]. As phages, viruses, plasmids, prions, viroids, and free DNA are usually not considered as living microorganisms [ 55 ], they do not belong to the microbiota.

span.label: mobile genetic elements
span.quote: The term microbiome, as it was originally postulated by Whipps and coworkers [ 40 ], includes not only the community of the microorganisms, but also their “theatre of activity.” The latter involves the whole spectrum of molecules produced by the microorganisms, including their structural elements (nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, polysaccharides), metabolites (signaling molecules, toxins, organic, and inorganic molecules), and molecules produced by coexisting hosts and structured by the surrounding environmental conditions. Therefore, all mobile genetic elements, such as phages, viruses, and “relic” and extracellular DNA, should be included in the term microbiome, but are not a part of microbiota

span.quote: There is also no clear consensus as to whether extracellular DNA derived from dead cells (so-called “relic DNA”) belongs to the microbiome. span.label: `microbiome` (Whipps et al. 1988, revived here) - `a CHARACTERISTIC MICROBIAL COMMUNITY occupying a reasonable well-defined habitat which has DISTINCT PHYSIO-CHEMICAL PROPERTIES ... not only refers to the microorganisms involved but also ENCOMPASS THEIR THEATRE OF ACTIVITY`
span.quote: The microbiome is defined as a characteristic microbial community occupying a reasonable well-defined habitat which has distinct physio-chemical properties. The microbiome not only refers to the microorganisms involved but also encompass their theatre of activity, which results in the formation of specific ecological niches. The microbiome, which forms a dynamic and interactive micro-ecosystem prone to change in time and scale, is integrated in macro-ecosystems including eukaryotic hosts, and here crucial for their functioning and health. The microbiota consists of the assembly of microorganisms belonging to different kingdoms (Prokaryotes [Bacteria, Archaea], Eukaryotes [e.g., Protozoa, Fungi, and Algae]), while “their theatre of activity” includes microbial structures, metabolites, mobile genetic elements (e.g., transposons, phages, and viruses), and relic DNA embedded in the environmental conditions of the habitat.

span.label: `microbiome` (Lederberg, THE MOST CITED) - `a community of commensal, symbiotic, and pathogenic microorganisms WITHIN A BODY SPACE OR OTHER ENVIRONMENT` - ecological, host-centred, and not the original
span.quote: The currently most cited definition by Lederberg [ 42 ] describes microbiomes within an ecological context, as a community of commensal, symbiotic, and pathogenic microorganisms within a body space or other environment. Marchesi and Ravel focused in their definition on the genomes and microbial (and viral) gene expression patterns and proteomes in a given environment and its prevailing biotic and abiotic conditions

span.quote: Despite more and more terms like “bacteriome,” “archaeome,” “mycobiome,” or “virome” have started to appear in the scientific literature, and these terms do not refer to biomes (a regional ecosystem with a distinct assemblage of (micro) organisms, and physical environment often reflecting a certain climate and soil) as the microbiome itself. Consequently, it would be better to use the original terms (bacterial, archaeal, or fungal community).

span.label: `a CHARACTERISTIC MICROBIAL COMMUNITY occupying a reasonable well-defined habitat which has DISTINCT PHYSIO-CHEMICAL PROPERTIES ... not only refers to the microorganisms involved but also ENCOMPASS THEIR THEATRE OF ACTIVITY, which results in the formation of specific ecological niches`
span.quote: The microbiome is defined as a characteristic microbial community occupying a reasonable well-defined habitat which has distinct physio-chemical properties. The microbiome not only refers to the microorganisms involved but also encompass their theatre of activity, which results in the formation of specific ecological niches. The microbiome, which forms a dynamic and interactive micro-ecosystem prone to change in time and scale, is integrated in macro-ecosystems including eukaryotic hosts, and here crucial for their functioning and health. The microbiota consists of the assembly of microorganisms belonging to different kingdoms (Prokaryotes [Bacteria, Archaea], Eukaryotes [e.g., Protozoa, Fungi, and Algae]), while “their theatre of activity” includes microbial structures, metabolites, mobile genetic elements (e.g., transposons, phages, and viruses), and relic DNA embedded in the environmental conditions of the habitat.

span.label: `the ASSEMBLAGE OF LIVING MICROORGANISMS present in a defined environment` - excluding phages, viruses, plasmids, prions, viroids and free DNA, which `are USUALLY NOT CONSIDERED AS LIVING MICROORGANISMS`
span.quote: When it comes to the use of specific terms, a clear differentiation between microbiome and microbiota helps to avoid the controversy concerning the members of a microbiome (Fig. 2 ). Microbiota is usually defined as the assemblage of living microorganisms present in a defined environment [ 25 ]. As phages, viruses, plasmids, prions, viroids, and free DNA are usually not considered as living microorganisms [ 55 ], they do not belong to the microbiota.

span.label: `a collection of genomes and genes from the members of a microbiota` - and the term microbiome `is also sometimes CONFUSED` with it
span.quote: The term microbiome is also sometimes confused with the metagenome. Metagenome is, however, clearly defined as a collection of genomes and genes from the members of a microbiota

span.term: spread of expert opinion on whether viruses belong
span.quote: The integration of phages, viruses, plasmids, and mobile genetic elements is one of the most controversial points in the definition of the microbiome. This was also confirmed by the participants’ comments in the “microbiome definition” online survey. The answers of the survey participants to the question whether viruses and phages should be a part of the microbiome provided no clear answer and stretched from “in any case” to “definitely no.”

span.label: `VALID EVEN 30 YEARS AFTER ITS PUBLICATION`, extended by two sentences
span.quote: Based on the recent advances in the area, we suggest the revival of the original definition of the microbiome term suggested by Whipps et al. [ 40 ]. The definition, which contains all important points that are valid even 30 years after its publication in 1988, was extended by two explanatory sentences differentiating the terms microbiome and microbiota and pronouncing its dynamic character.

span.label: Whipps' phrase for everything that is not the organisms - structural elements, metabolites, mobile genetic elements and relic DNA in the habitat's conditions - and the half of the term that the genomic definitions drop
span.quote: The term microbiome, as it was originally postulated by Whipps and coworkers [ 40 ], includes not only the community of the microorganisms, but also their “theatre of activity.” The latter involves the whole spectrum of molecules produced by the microorganisms, including their structural elements (nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, polysaccharides), metabolites (signaling molecules, toxins, organic, and inorganic molecules), and molecules produced by coexisting hosts and structured by the surrounding environmental conditions. Therefore, all mobile genetic elements, such as phages, viruses, and “relic” and extracellular DNA, should be included in the term microbiome, but are not a part of microbiota
